fichas.title: Principles of sun protection
fichas.summary: Sun protection and daylight-direction systems aim to limit excessive heat radiation and glare while allowing individual user control and avoiding interference with ventilation. The page illustrates facade-side light incidence, rooflight entry, and natural sun protection from deciduous trees, which shade in summer and admit warmth and light in winter.

fichas.title: Sun angles and projection of sun-protection components
fichas.summary: The page gives solar-angle examples for a south wall at a northern latitude below 50° and describes calculating the projection of a sun-protection component from the shadow angle and window height, with a wall-thickness adjustment and a stated minimum projection. The formula is retained symbolically; no unprinted values are calculated.
uses: Relate seasonal sun angles to shading design

dimensions.label: Northern latitude threshold
dimensions.context: The stated solar-angle guidance applies to a south wall at a northern latitude less than this threshold.

Natural sun protection
Deciduous trees offer natural
sun protection in summer. In
winter, the leafless trees allow
warmth and light into the
room.
Systems
System selection
depends
mainly on the compass direction of the window to be protected. On north sides, direct
sunshine can only be expected
in the mornings in June and July
and simple internal systems are
sufficient. If the alignment is
largely west or east, movable
systems should shade the low
sun.

South windows need effective
shading above all in the early
year and autumn, with low
sun. In the high summer, slight
roof overhangs are sufficient to
avoid direct sunshine.

fichas.title: Sun-shading systems and selection
fichas.summary: The page surveys shutters, external blinds, inter-pane shading, vertical blades, awnings, roof overhangs, and double facades. System selection depends mainly on window orientation: movable systems are recommended for low east and west sun, while slight roof overhangs can suffice against high summer sun on south windows. External closed shading needs a route for heat to escape; systems close to windows can risk overheating or impair ventilation.
